title: Determinants of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 Matrices
short: ad − bc, and expansion by minors.
trouble: Students compute ad + bc, or lose the alternating signs in a 3 × 3 expansion.

blocks.html: Every square matrix has a single number attached to it, its determinant. It tells you whether a system has a unique solution, whether a matrix has an inverse, and how a transformation changes area. It grows out of matrix arithmetic and elimination.

$$\det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.$$ For a $3 \times 3$ matrix, expand along the first row with the signs $+, -, +$: each entry times the $2 \times 2$ determinant left when you cross out its row and column (its minor).

Solve $ax + by = e$, $cx + dy = f$ by elimination: multiply the first equation by $d$ and the second by $b$, then subtract. You get $(ad - bc)x = ed - bf$. If $ad - bc \ne 0$ you can divide, and there is exactly one solution; if $ad - bc = 0$ you cannot. Geometrically, $|ad - bc|$ is the area of the parallelogram formed by the columns $\langle a, c \rangle$ and $\langle b, d \rangle$.

blocks.name: matrix2d
blocks.cap: The unit square becomes a parallelogram whose area is $|\det|$. Try a matrix with determinant $0$: the square collapses onto a line.

blocks.title: When is it zero?
steps: Then the rows $(3, 6)$ and $(2, 4)$ are proportional, so the system they describe has no unique solution.

blocks.html: Computing $ad + bc$, or losing the alternating signs in a $3 \times 3$ expansion. For $2 \times 2$: main diagonal product minus the other diagonal product. For $3 \times 3$: the signs follow the checkerboard $\begin{bmatrix} + & - & + \\ - & + & - \\ + & - & + \end{bmatrix}$. A quick check: swapping two rows should change the sign of the determinant.
